#6402. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

#6400. “Schrödinger’s Penguin”: Scientists Discover a Bizarre Paradox Among Endangered Penguins

Endangered erect-crested penguins are holding steady on tiny islands while declining on a breeding ground 40 times larger, challenging assumptions about where the species’ best hope for survival lies.

An endangered penguin species could receive a less severe global risk rating even as one of its only two breeding populations suffers a steep decline. A survey of erect-crested penguins in Aotearoa New Zealand shows how a single assessment of an entire species can conceal very different conservation needs.

The erect-crested penguin is among just four penguin species worldwide listed as “Endangered” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another is New Zealand’s hoiho, or yellow-eyed penguin. Yet while the hoiho has attracted sustained public and conservation attention, the erect-crested penguin remains largely overlooked and is one of the country’s least-studied penguin species.

These birds breed only on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two remote island groups about 800 kilometers (500 miles) southeast of the South Island. Between 2022 and 2024, researchers used drones to photograph and count every breeding colony across both groups, the first time this had been done for the entire species.

The study, published October 21, 2026, in PLOS ONE, was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, whose researchers are based in the Departments of Zoology and Marine Science at the University of Otago (Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka). The team collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Mattern says, “Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

“The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995.”

The counts also challenged the historical view of where most of the species breeds.

“The results overturn a long-standing assumption,” Mattern says.

“The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species’ stronghold.”

The researchers have dubbed the situation “Schrödinger’s Penguin” after the well-known thought experiment in which a cat sealed in a box is imagined to be simultaneously alive and dead until someone opens it and checks. For the penguins, Mattern says, the logic runs in reverse.

“With Schrödinger’s cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

“With Erect-crested penguins, it’s the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

“Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn’t one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands.”

On the Antipodes Islands, a shrinking colony may become increasingly difficult for the penguins to defend. Mattern describes how that can compound the losses.

“As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further.”

The islands’ eastern rockhopper penguins had already experienced a population collapse. Their numbers crashed “catastrophically” during the second half of the 20th century, leaving fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs on the Antipodes Islands. The decline mirrored trends elsewhere across the species’ Southern Ocean breeding range and was likely driven by ocean warming.

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that this loss may have changed which penguins the predators targeted.

“As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead,” Pütz says.

Increasingly severe storms, consistent with broader climate trends in the Southern Ocean, have also triggered landslides that break colonies into smaller fragments and put them at further risk. Differences in the birds’ ocean habitats and migration routes likely add to the pressures.

Outside the breeding season, Antipodes birds travel far into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone, a region of the Southern Ocean, Mattern says. Bounty Islands birds stay close to their breeding sites in more sheltered waters that may also be more productive.

The contrasting population histories complicate how the species’ extinction risk should be assessed. According to Mattern, its current Endangered ranking rests on inflated population estimates from the 1970s. Reassessing that status against the new data broadly supports the ranking for the Antipodes population, but not for the Bounty population.

“Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to “Vulnerable”, masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species’ last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing.

“A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger’s box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs,” Mattern says.

Reference: “Schrödinger’s Penguin? Divergent population trajectories and the challenge of assessing the threat status of the Erect-crested penguin” by Thomas Mattern, Klemens Pütz, Hannah Mattern, Robin Long, Dave Houston, Bianca Keys, Jeff White, Richard Seed, Myrene Otis, Ursula Ellenberg, Pablo Garcia-Borboroglu and Benno Lüthi, 21 October 2026, PLOS ONE. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0359075

The study was funded by the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust, the Global Penguin Society, and conducted under permits from the New Zealand Department of Conservation.

Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.

The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.

Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.

Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.

First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).

The geological profile of Tell el-Fara'in (ancient Buto) and the surrounding Nile Delta, showing the layered sequence of river sands and flood-plain clays from the last ice age and the settlement mound above.

To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.

The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment.

Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.

And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.

That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.

The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.

A 2D electrical resistivity scan aligned with a partially exposed mudbrick wall — the colored subsurface anomaly matches the location of the visible structure above ground.

"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."

The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.

A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.

The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.

"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."

The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Abouarab, M. a. R., Elfadaly, A., Elbehery, W., Wafa, O., Aboalkassim, I., Younes, A., Hiekl, A. M. A., Saada, S. A., Wilson, P., & Ibrahim, A. (2026). Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4

#6397. New Research Reveals That Honey Beehives Act as a Living Immune System

Scientists have discovered that honey beehives possess a surprisingly sophisticated system for protecting colonies against disease.

A honey bee colony relies on more than its workers to fight disease. The hive itself acts as a “living immune system,” using carefully arranged natural materials to create layers of antimicrobial protection around developing bees and stored food. New research shows that these defenses are closely linked to the surrounding landscape, with local vegetation influencing how effectively a colony can resist harmful microbes.

“Hives are not only homes for bees, but also act as their workplaces, restaurants, and hospitals, and now we can add immune systems to the list,” said lead researcher Dr. Kenya Fernandes.

The strongest antimicrobial defenses were found in parts of the hive most exposed to the outside environment. Honey showed particularly powerful antimicrobial activity, while propolis, a sticky plant-derived substance bees use to seal cracks and openings, provided additional protection. Both materials contained biologically active compounds, including hydrogen peroxide in honey and plant chemicals called flavonoids in propolis.

Deeper inside the hive, where eggs and larvae develop, the defenses became more selective. Beeswax combs, stored pollen, and substances produced by the bees themselves helped suppress harmful bacteria and fungi while supporting beneficial microbial communities.

“As we travel closer to the hive center, the antimicrobial defenses became more targeted, with wax comb, stored pollen, and the bee’s own bodies helping to filter out harmful bacteria and fungi, while encouraging helpful species,” said Fernandes, a 2026 NSW Tall Young Poppy Award recipient.

“We already know honey, beeswax and propolis have antimicrobial properties independently. But what came as a surprise was how these materials were placed in the hive wasn’t random, but organized. The hive’s antimicrobial properties worked together to protect the eggs and larvae, as well as the fermented pollen the bees consume.”

For the study, published in ISME Communications, scientists examined 24 honey bee colonies across five apiaries at Tocal College in New South Wales, Australia. They analyzed the chemical composition and antimicrobial properties of honey, pollen, beeswax, and propolis. They also investigated microbes living in the bees’ digestive systems and tested the antimicrobial activity of their tissues and secretions.

The researchers found that many microorganisms in hive materials likely originated from floral nectar. Colonies located closer to native bushland also showed measurable differences in chemical defenses compared with those near agricultural land. These differences suggest that the plants available to foraging bees influence the protective properties of the materials they bring home.

“This shows healthy hives depend on and are influenced by healthy ecosystems. Land clearing and intensive farming could be quietly eroding the bees’ natural defenses. This builds a strong case for protecting diverse flowering habitats that support healthy hives,” said co-author Elizabeth Frost, Technical Specialist Bees at the NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD).

The hive’s protective system was generally more effective against bacteria than fungi. Researchers suggest this imbalance may reflect the greater threat posed by certain bacterial infections. One example is American foulbrood, a highly contagious disease that kills honeybee larvae and can destroy entire colonies.

“There are direct threats to bee populations such as the varroa mite, but many don’t realize the indirect threats: the shrinking of healthy ecosystems has a domino effect. Landscapes with diverse plant species can increase the bees’ chances of being resilient to disease.”

The findings also raise questions about other colony-building insects. Although the study focused on European honey bees, Fernandes hopes to investigate whether Australian native stingless bees have comparable nest-based defenses and whether similar systems occur in other social insects.

“I’d love to see if other social insects such as native stingless bees, ants, and termites, which also build incredibly complex homes, also have the same system,” Fernandes said.

Reference: “Spatially organized chemical defences shape microbial communities in honey bee colonies” by Kenya E Fernandes, Aviva Levina, Elizabeth A Frost and Dee A Carter, 19 October 2026, ISME Communications. DOI: 10.1093/ismeco/ycag247

Funding: Australian Research Council, New South Wales Bushfire Industry Recovery Package Sector Development Grant

#6395. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

#6392. Scientists Sound the Alarm As Colorectal Cancer Reverses a 20-Year Decline

Colorectal cancer rates in the United States are rising across a much wider range of ages than previously recognized, reversing a long period of declining diagnoses. A new study published in NEJM Evidence found that the increase is no longer concentrated among adults younger than 50, with rates now climbing in people approaching their 70s.

Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths overall in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. As more generations reach ages when the disease becomes increasingly common, researchers warn that growing numbers of diagnoses could place additional demands on cancer treatment and long-term survivorship care.

Researchers led by Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, analyzed National Cancer Institute data to track changes in colorectal cancer incidence over more than two decades. The age-adjusted rate dropped from 55.2 cases per 100,000 people in 2000 to 36.7 in 2022, before increasing to 38.3 in 2023.

“This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years,” Murphy said. The study also found rising incidence across age groups through 65 to 69 years, indicating that the trend extends well beyond the younger populations that have received much of the attention.

The increase among older adults is particularly concerning because colorectal cancer screening has historically produced substantial benefits in these age groups. Rates are now rising among people ages 65 to 69 and have stopped declining among those ages 70 to 74, despite approximately 80% of people in these groups being up to date with screening. Researchers suspect that unidentified risk factors may be counteracting some of the progress achieved through earlier detection and prevention.

Murphy believes the expanding age range reflects a phenomenon known as the “birth cohort effect,” in which people born during particular periods experience different disease risks as they grow older. In this case, evidence suggests that individuals born in the 1960s and afterward may face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer that persists as they advance into middle and older adulthood.

“I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time,” Murphy explained. “As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we’re going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.”

The pattern could help connect the growing incidence among younger adults with the increases now appearing in older populations. American Cancer Society statistics show that colorectal cancer incidence among people ages 20 to 49 rose approximately 3% annually from 2013 to 2022.

“There are many unique challenges when you’re diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it’s important that we shine a spotlight on that problem,” Murphy said. “But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.”

The steepest increase occurred among adults ages 45 to 49, whose colorectal cancer incidence rose by 12.76% annually between 2019 and 2023. Researchers believe this unusually rapid increase largely reflects expanded screening following a change in national guidelines that lowered the recommended starting age from 50 to 45.

Screening can temporarily raise reported incidence by detecting cancers that were already present but had not yet been diagnosed. “That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do — it’s catching cancer earlier,” Murphy said.

However, increased screening cannot fully account for the broader rise across age groups, especially among older adults who already have high screening participation. The researchers also examined whether disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to the trend. The increase persisted even when data from 2020 and 2021 were excluded, and screening activity had largely returned to pre-pandemic levels by January 2021. These findings suggest that pandemic-related delays are unlikely to explain the overall increase observed in 2023.

The underlying causes of the rising incidence remain uncertain. Researchers are now examining whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could contribute to colorectal cancer risk, although no specific exposure has been established as responsible for the observed trends.

“These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced,” said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Murphy is collaborating with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to investigate thousands of environmental chemical exposures using small blood samples. This approach will help identify substances that may warrant closer examination.

The researchers then plan to work with Kupfer to study selected chemicals using colon organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce some features of human colon tissue. These models will allow scientists to investigate how particular exposures affect colon cells and potentially identify biological processes involved in cancer development.

Until the causes become clearer, colorectal cancer screening remains one of the most effective ways to identify the disease early and prevent deaths. Current national guidelines recommend routine screening for adults at average risk beginning at age 45 and continuing through age 75. Screening decisions outside that range should be individualized based on factors such as family history, symptoms, and other medical conditions.

Colonoscopy remains the gold standard because it can both detect cancer and remove precancerous polyps. Other screening methods include home-based stool tests and newer blood-based tests, although their capabilities and recommended testing intervals differ.

“There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated,” Kupfer added.

For adults younger than 45 who do not qualify for routine screening, recognizing possible warning signs is particularly important. Blood in the stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, and unexplained weight loss should prompt medical evaluation, even in people without a known family history or genetic risk.

The research team also recommends continued monitoring of national cancer registry data as new figures become available. If the upward trend persists as large generations of Americans grow older, healthcare systems may face increasing demand for cancer treatment, follow-up care, and long-term support for survivors.

Reference: “Colorectal Cancer among U.S. Adults, 2000–2023” by Caitlin C. Murphy, Folasade P. May, Sonia S. Kupfer, Xin Hu and Samir Gupta, 27 October 2026, NEJM Evidence. DOI: 10.1056/EVIDpha2600217

The study was supported by funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

#6390. A Hidden Cancer-Fighting Switch Could Supercharge the Human Immune System

Temporarily activating a protein best known for preventing cancer helped engineered human immune cells kill melanoma cells more effectively in the lab, suggesting a way to improve existing cell therapies.

Engineering a patient’s immune cells to recognize cancer does not guarantee that they will keep fighting it. Repeated exposure to cancer can gradually weaken T cells’ ability to multiply and attack tumors, a decline known as exhaustion. The laboratory process used to prepare these cells for treatment can also make them mature too quickly, reducing their chances of surviving and remaining effective over time.

These problems limit engineered T-cell therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy and T-cell receptor (TCR) therapy. Both involve collecting a patient’s immune cells, genetically modifying them in a laboratory to recognize cancer, and infusing them back into the patient to attack tumors. Such treatments have transformed care for certain blood cancers and are increasingly being investigated for solid tumors.

Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have identified a possible way to improve these cells during preparation. Their study, published in Frontiers in Immunology, found that temporarily activating a protein called p53 helped human T cells develop characteristics associated with longer-lasting immune responses and become more effective at killing melanoma cells in the laboratory.

Often called the “guardian of the genome,” p53 is best known for preventing damaged cells from becoming cancerous. Scientists have extensively studied that protective role, but its involvement in regulating human T cells is less understood.

The team collected human T cells and treated them with navtemadlin, an investigational drug that increases p53 activity by blocking another protein, MDM2. Normally, MDM2 keeps p53 levels under control. Comparing treated and untreated cells allowed the researchers to assess how activating p53 affected their development, energy production, and ability to fight cancer.

To test cancer-killing performance, the researchers genetically engineered T cells to recognize a protein found on certain melanoma cells. They then used specialized imaging equipment to monitor the cells for nearly seven days.

The engineered T cells prepared with navtemadlin were significantly more effective at killing melanoma cells than untreated cells. Their advantage became apparent after approximately 40 hours and continued throughout the experiment. They also showed improved cancer-fighting activity without additional interleukin-2, a protein commonly used to support T-cell growth and survival.

“This is one of the first studies to link p53, one of the most extensively studied proteins in biology, to T-cell exhaustion in humans,” said Joseph Crompton, MD, PhD, assistant professor of surgery at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and senior author of the study. “While p53 has long been known for its role in preventing cancer, our findings suggest it may also play an important role in helping immune cells maintain their ability to fight it. This opens up a new avenue for developing more effective cancer immunotherapies.”

The treated cells had greater energy reserves and were more likely to produce interferon-gamma and granzyme B, two cancer-fighting proteins that help immune cells coordinate an attack and destroy cancer cells.

They were also more likely to develop into central memory T cells, which have a greater capacity to survive and multiply when they encounter their target again. Along with fewer molecular signs of exhaustion, this shift suggested that the cells might remain effective for longer. Those characteristics indicate potential for lasting immune responses, although the experiments tested human cells in the laboratory rather than treatment outcomes in patients.

Adding a drug such as navtemadlin during cell preparation could potentially fit into existing manufacturing processes. That would offer a way to improve engineered T-cell therapies without developing an entirely new treatment or introducing additional genetic modifications.

At lower concentrations, navtemadlin encouraged the development of healthy memory T cells without substantially reducing the overall number of viable cells. Higher concentrations, however, caused more cells to die, showing why any use of this approach would require careful control of p53 activation.

Reference: “p53 activation via pharmacologic MDM2 inhibition constrains exhaustion and enhances antitumor function of human CD8+ T cells” by Alexandra Boix de Jesus, Hy B. Gomperts, Tyler R. McCaw, Cristina Puig-Saus and Joseph G. Crompton, 18 September 2026, Frontiers in Immunology. DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2026.1910235

Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.

In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.

The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.

"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."

The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?

To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.

"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."

The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.

Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats ‪—‬ thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.

An illustration of a microbial mat covering A. museunacionali's bones after it died.

"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."

The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.

While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.

"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."

For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.

According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.

"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

Editor's Note: This article was updated at 5:44 p.m. E.D.T. to remove an outside comment that suggested the study did not include resonance Raman spectroscopy. The team did perform that analysis.

O., Demore, J., Saraiva, A. a. F., Rickard, W. D. A., Ohkouchi, N., Sayão, J. M., . . . Kellner, A. W. A. (2026). Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(0), e2614248123. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2614248123

#6386. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

This story was updated on October 29, 2026 to include expert input from Emma Stone.

#6383. Study Reveals How Brain Function Changes When We Learn Something New

A beginner’s violin lesson may seem worlds apart from dementia research, yet wearable brain scans are revealing signals that could help scientists understand both learning and neurological disease.

Playing a familiar tune on a violin is no simple task for someone who has never held the instrument. Each movement must produce the intended sound, and the brain has to learn how to coordinate those movements. Researchers at the University of Nottingham have now captured changes in brain activity as beginners learned to play, revealing measurable differences after just one violin lesson.

The study, published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience, involved 22 novice violin players. Using a wearable brain scanner, the scientists tracked patterns of neural activity while participants attempted to play “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They found that those who improved the most also showed the greatest changes in certain brain signals associated with movement and learning.

Capturing those signals while someone plays an instrument presents a technical challenge. The electrical activity of neurons generates extremely weak magnetic fields, which can be measured to study brain function. However, the equipment must be sensitive enough to detect these signals without interference, while still allowing the person being studied to move naturally.

The researchers used a technology called OPM-MEG, developed in Nottingham, that incorporates brain-scanning sensors into a lightweight helmet connected to a backpack-mounted control unit. Unlike scanning systems that restrict movement, this wearable design allows researchers to monitor brain activity as people perform everyday tasks.

There was still one problem. A conventional violin contains metal components that would interfere with the scanner’s measurements.

To overcome this obstacle, the team enlisted Alan Kirby, an expert violinist and violin maker from Nottingham. Kirby sourced a standard violin and replaced every metal part with alternatives he crafted himself, producing an entirely wooden instrument operating at frequencies associated with Baroque music.

“Bringing together the ancient art of violin making, with the quantum physics underpinning this brain scanner, has been amazing. Perhaps even more impressive was to actually see the effects of my lessons on peoples brains. That was quite an experience,” Kirby said.

Kirby also served as the participants’ violin instructor. At the beginning of the experiment, all 22 beginners watched a video of him playing “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star.” They then attempted to perform the same melody during their first scanning session, while the researchers recorded their brain activity.

After completing that initial recording, the participants received a violin lesson from Kirby. They then returned for a second scanning session, following the same procedure and attempting to play the tune again. By comparing recordings from before and after the lesson, the researchers could examine how the brain responded to a brief period of musical training.

Their attention focused on brain waves, rhythmic fluctuations in electrical activity that occur across groups of neurons. In particular, they examined oscillations in the beta frequency range, which are thought to help signal whether an action produces the result the brain expects.

When learning the violin, that process could involve predicting the sound of a note before playing it and registering whether the actual sound matches the prediction. Unexpected notes provide information that the movement did not produce the intended outcome.

“Your brain works by making predictions about what will happen as a result of your actions. So, if I am playing a violin, my brain will have an expectation of what sound it will make. If I play the expected note, my brain receives information that the outcome matched its prediction; if I hit an unexpected note, it receives information that it did not. In this experiment, we were able to measure these signals in real time while the instrument was being played,” said Joe Gibson, a Ph.D. researcher in the School of Physics and Astronomy.

The recordings revealed changes in beta-wave activity following the lesson, providing evidence that even a short period of musical instruction can alter measurable patterns of brain function. The researchers also found a relationship between those neural changes and improvements in playing ability.

Participants with the largest differences in beta-wave activity between the two scanning sessions also showed the greatest improvement in their violin performance. Although the findings do not establish that the changes in brain activity caused better playing, they suggest that beta oscillations are closely associated with how people acquire new motor skills.

Making these measurements possible required expertise extending well beyond neuroscience. Professor Matthew Brookes of the University of Nottingham’s School of Physics and Astronomy has spent more than a decade leading the development of OPM-MEG technology. The violin experiment brought together specialists in physics, engineering, mathematics, and music to create a system capable of studying movement as it happens.

“This is a study that we have been working on for years, and it’s taken a unique combination of skills: the physics required to measure brain activity; design engineering to create an ergonomic scanner that people can wear; the mathematics required to model the signals; and of course, Alan’s knowledge and abilities as a violin player and maker. Without this wonderful diversity of talent, we simply couldn’t have done the work.”

The researchers believe the technology could eventually help scientists investigate more than musical learning. Some of the patterns of brain activity measured during the experiment can also be affected by neurological conditions, including dementia. Studying these signals during natural movements could offer another way to examine how brain function changes in health and disease.

“The results provide a greater understanding of motor learning. It’s also fascinating that some of the effects that we measure here are among those that can be affected by disorders like dementia. Hopefully this type of study will bring about a new understanding of not just healthy brain function, but also disease,” said Brookes.

Reference: “Beta-band dynamics during a naturalistic motor task: an OPM-MEG study” by Joseph Gibson, Jessikah Fildes, Alan Kirby, Niall Holmes, Lukas Rier, Karen J. Mullinger, Matias Ison, Peter G. Morris, Elena Boto, Ryan M. Hill and Matthew J. Brookes, 27 July 2026, bioRxiv. DOI: 10.64898/2026.07.27.740561

Disclosure: The University launched a spin-out company, Cerca Magnetics Limited, in 2020 to commercialize OPM-MEG scanners and related technologies. The wearable system has been installed in a number of high profile research institutions across the globe and is being used to investigate a range of neurological and psychiatric conditions, including epilepsy and dementia.

Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.

"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.

"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.

Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.

The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter ‪—‬ one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder ‪—‬ it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.

Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, 18(10), 209. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12520-026-02574-7

#6378. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints.

The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One, found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis, which is known to increase the risk of heart failure.

This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation.

But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats (80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth.

"The message that we try to convey … is that the follow-up time is really important," study co-author John Baker, a professor of surgery in the Radiation Bioscience Laboratory at the Medical College of Wisconsin, told Live Science. "When astronauts come back to the Earth, they expect ‪—‬ and we expect ‪—‬ that they're going to live for a long time. I think we have to be wary that they could well develop at least some type of cardiac disease."

The link between exposure to radiation and cardiac issues has been well documented. However, "no astronaut has ever been exposed to galactic cosmic radiation for long periods of time," Baker said, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how space radiation affects the heart.

Although Baker and his team previously pinpointed cardiac issues among rats exposed to radiation, this new study utilized NASA's Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Simulation (SimGCRSim). This new simulator provides a more precise comparison of the levels of space radiation an astronaut might experience while exploring deep space for more than a year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

During the study, the researchers exposed rats to several minutes of radiation proportionate to their size, similar to what they might experience on a trip to Mars and back (a roughly 18-month round trip, with current technology). Some of the rats' hind legs were suspended, to "simulate conditions of weightlessness," Baker said.

After 360 days, the rats that were exposed to cosmic radiation developed twice as much scar tissue around the heart's small blood vessels than unexposed rats. This buildup of scar tissue means "the heart can't relax to the point when it needs to," thereby increasing the risk of heart failure, Baker said.

This effect was not seen in the rats who were exposed only to simulated weightlessness, confirming "it was only the radiation that produced the damaging effect on the heart," Baker said. However, long-term testing revealed that this group of rats had lower levels of key immune cells, suggesting that microgravity also may affect aspects of long-term health. (Numerous studies have shown various short-term health impacts related to microgravity.)

This study "is a very valuable contribution to space biology," Rupak Pathak, an associate professor of pharmaceutical science at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences who was not involved in the study but holds a doctorate in radiation biology, told Live Science. While rats and humans have clear differences, "they share more than 90% of genetic information," he said, as well as very similar cardiac systems.

Given that the study authors were able to expose the rats to radiation only once, Pathak would like to see further experiments exploring whether chronic radiation exposure affects the function of the heart and other vital organs.

Baker and his colleagues hope that future experiments can be used to help NASA implement safeguards for astronauts on long-term missions, such as providing astronauts heart medications or improving shielding for the spacecraft.

"The more we know before we start, then the better NASA is going to be at working out what types of countermeasures can be developed," said Baker.

#6372. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photos? Space debris from a Russian rocket burning up upon reentry

Who took the photos? NASA astronaut Chris Williams

Earlier this year, an astronaut on board the International Space Station (ISS) snapped some striking photos, and an eerily beautiful video, of a "fireball" streaking over Earth as chunks of space debris burned up in the nighttime sky.

NASA's Chris Williams, who lived and worked on the ISS between November 2025 and July 2026, captured the eye-catching images from the station's cupola — a large, roughly dome-shaped series of windows that constantly points down at our planet — and later shared them on the social media platform X.

"Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," Williams wrote in the post. "I saw its tail grow and then split apart into a shower of smaller pieces," he added. "It was quite a light show!"

Williams initially peered down at Earth to catch a glimpse of the Russian cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which successfully delivered essential supplies and additional equipment to the ISS later the same day. Instead, he saw what he believed was "some piece of orbital debris or a satellite breaking up as it entered the atmosphere."

Live Science's sister site Space.com later revealed that Williams had actually witnessed the burning remains of the Russian Soyuz rocket that had carried Progress 95 into space, after it lifted off from a recently repaired launchpad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The Soyuz rocket launched the cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which later docked with the ISS. (This photo shows the Progress 46 mission docking with the station in 2011.)

Shortly after deploying the resupply shuttle into low Earth orbit, the rocket's fairings and booster fell back toward our planet as expected, breaking apart into smaller pieces that were superheated and later vaporized by intense friction as they hit the upper atmosphere, according to Space.com. A very similar fireball was seen above Australia in August 2023, when another Soyuz rocket reentered the atmosphere.

Russia's prior resupply mission, Progress 94, also made headlines earlier this year when one of its antennae failed to deploy after separation from its Soyuz rocket, forcing cosmonauts (Russian astronauts) to use a remote control "backup system" to dock the spacecraft to the ISS.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Historically, the only fireballs visible in Earth's skies have been those caused by meteors, which can similarly break apart in flames. We were recently reminded of this when fireballs were spotted above the U.S. this spring, including one space rock that exploded with a massive sonic boom over Ohio and another that crashed through the roof of a house in Houston. (A NASA statement said the fireball Williams witnessed also may have been caused by meteor activity but was more likely to be the Soyuz rocket.)

However, fireballs from human-made objects are becoming more common. The number of spacecraft orbiting Earth has skyrocketed (pun intended) in recent decades, and "what goes up must come down."

Williams' photographs show how the remains of the Soyuz rocket exploded in a bright flash before stretching out into a train of flaming debris.

Most spacecraft and large pieces of space junk burn up around 50 miles (80 kilometers) above Earth's surface — just below the imaginary boundary with space, known as the Kármán line. While this may lead to visually stunning spectacles like the one Williams captured, scientists are starting to realize that these fireballs may be having a bigger impact on the upper atmosphere than they previously expected.

In recent years, researchers have detected a sharp increase in atmospheric metal pollution from vaporized spacecraft. And while they are still trying to figure out what effect this may have, some scientists have proposed that it could affect the ozone layer or potentially alter Earth's magnetic field.

Additionally, as the number of falling spacecraft rises, the chances that debris may fall to Earth's surface — after failing to properly burn up upon reentry — also increase. This came to the fore in March 2024, when the remains of a 3-ton battery pack that was discarded from the ISS crashed into a family home in Florida.

This 2011 astronaut photo captured one of NASA's iconic space shuttles passing between Earth and the International Space Station for the very last time.

During the Sept. 11 attacks, NASA astronaut Frank Culbertson — the only American not on Earth at the time — snapped a "sobering" shot of smoke pouring across New York City as the second tower fell.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology.
