#6352. Forests planted to fight climate change may be fueling wildfires

A global study reveals that planting forests can increase wildfire risk, threatening carbon storage and challenging climate strategies.

There’s something darkly ironic about planting a forest to store carbon and watching it go up in flames.

But new research suggests that planting trees can sometimes increase wildfire risk, threatening the very carbon those forests were meant to store.

A new global study reveals just how much that risk varies across different landscapes.

An international team of researchers from Spain, Chile, and Finland analyzed satellite records spanning more than two decades to track what happens when non-forested land gets converted into planted forests.

Their dataset was enormous: 67,248 patches across the world’s temperate regions, monitored from 2001 to 2023 using MODIS land-cover and fire records.

After accounting for climate, accessibility, and patch size, afforestation was associated with a 26% increase in fire occurrence per hectare per year and a 23% increase in expected burned area when fires did ignite.

“Forest plantations change the fuel conditions in which fires start and spread,” said lead author Irene Repeto-Deudero from the University of Cádiz and the University of Eastern Finland.

“We wanted to understand how these changes differ across landscapes, rather than assuming that tree planting has the same consequences everywhere.”

Those global averages, though, hide enormous variation. The researchers compared fire patterns across four major types of temperate landscapes.

Temperate conifer forests took the worst hit. Fire occurrence there surged 2.7-fold, and the expected burned area roughly doubled.

These landscapes already contain large amounts of vegetation and face increasingly extreme fire weather.

Adding dense plantations can create more continuous fuel, allowing fires to spread more easily.

Mediterranean forests, woodlands, and scrub saw a 38% jump in fire occurrence and a 9% rise in burned area. In absolute terms, the probability of fire per 100 hectares over a decade climbed from 7.8% to 11.0%.

These regions already contend with seasonal drought, flammable vegetation, and frequent human-caused ignitions.

Piling more biomass onto that tinderbox gives extreme fire weather more fuel to work with.

Temperate broadleaf and mixed forests told a stranger story. Fire occurrence actually dropped by 23% after afforestation – but expected burned area grew by 20%.

Fewer fires, in other words, but the ones that did ignite burned larger. That trade-off matters more than it might seem.

Nearly half of the world’s planted forests sit in this biome. Even modest shifts in fire behavior could carry substantial consequences.

Temperate grasslands, savannas, and shrublands were the one bright spot. There, fire occurrence fell 18% with no significant increase in burned area.

“These contrasting responses show why local ecological conditions must guide afforestation decisions,” explained study co-author Alejandro Miranda from the University of La Frontera.

“The same intervention can have very different consequences depending on the vegetation, climate, and existing fire regime.”

Geographically, the increases in wildfire activity clustered in regions that are already under fire stress.

These include western North America, central Chile, southern Europe, southwestern Australia, and parts of South Africa.

In these regions, expanding plantations and increasingly dangerous fire weather could combine to intensify wildfire risks.

The study also highlights a data point that deserves more attention. Plantations are roughly twice as likely to burn as native temperate forests.

And monoculture plantations – single-species stands planted in uniform rows – have been linked to particularly extreme fire behavior.

All of this creates a serious accounting problem for climate policy.

Afforestation has become a flagship mitigation strategy, with temperate regions identified as high-priority planting zones.

But wildfires don’t just destroy trees. They also release stored carbon back into the atmosphere, potentially reducing or even reversing the climate benefits of tree planting.

“These results therefore require that tree planting initiatives consider their exposure to fire,” said Susana Gómez-González from the University of Cádiz.

“As the climate warms, increased wildfire risk may impact the capacity of forest plantations to store carbon in the long term.”

Planted forests provide wood, protect soil, and deliver a range of ecosystem services. The point isn’t to stop – it’s to think harder about where to plant them.

“Plantations are necessary in many cases to produce wood and other ecosystem services, including soil protection,” said Blas Mola-Yudego from the University of Eastern Finland.

“However, their location must be carefully planned to avoid unintended consequences on local fire regimes.”

“Fire risk needs to be considered from the outset, alongside production goals and environmental benefits.”

The findings challenge the assumption that planting more trees automatically delivers greater climate benefits.

In some landscapes, the additional wildfire risk could undermine the carbon gains that plantations are meant to provide.

For policymakers counting on planted forests to help combat climate change, the message is clear: where trees are planted may matter just as much as how many are planted.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

#6350. Eliminating invasive rats could help islands survive rising seas

Removing invasive rats could help protect low-lying islands from rising seas by restoring seabirds, boosting coral reef growth, and increasing sand production.

Low-lying atoll islands are usually written off as the first places a rising sea will cover. Around some of them, though, the coral reef is growing fast enough to keep pace with the sea through the end of this century.

One important factor is whether invasive rats have driven away the island’s seabirds.

Where seabirds nest, their droppings feed the reef.

Lagoon reefs there build upward almost twice as fast as reefs beside rat-overrun islands and produce more than twice as much sand.

Native forests produce more than four times as much fine root growth as areas dominated by coconut palms. This can hold the island’s soil in place.

Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University‘s Lancaster Environment Centre, led a team that measured all three factors on 28 islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

The team compared islands as they are today, with and without rats.

“Atoll islands are not static, they are naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” Graham said.

Boobies, frigatebirds, terns and noddies feed at sea, up to 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) from the island where they nest. They come home to roost, and the guano they deposit on the island contains nitrogen.

On islands with the largest seabird colonies, their droppings deposited more than 320 pounds of nitrogen per acre (366 kilograms per hectare) each year.

Rats that arrived on ships eat seabird eggs and chicks, and on most atolls the bird colonies are gone. Many islands have also lost their native forest to coconut plantations.

These palms now make up about 60 percent of the forest on Pacific atolls.

The team counted nests on islands in the Seychelles, the Chagos Archipelago and Tetiaroa Atoll in French Polynesia.

Islands with no rats and mostly native forest got the heaviest rain of bird nitrogen. The rest got very little.

Corals near seabird islands photosynthesized more and laid down more limestone skeleton. From that, the team estimated how fast each reef could build upward.

Lagoon reefs beside rat-free islands rose by an estimated 0.23 inches (5.9 millimeters) a year.

This is 1.8 times the rate of reef rise beside rat-infested islands. Ocean-facing reefs showed a smaller and less certain edge.

For the central Indian Ocean, the sea is projected to rise about 0.24 inches (6 millimeters) a year by 2100 if the world warms by 2°C (3.6°F).

The bird-fed lagoon reefs could nearly match that. The reefs beside rat islands, however, are predicted to fall short of even today’s rise of about 0.16 inches (4 millimeters) a year.

A reef that keeps pace with rising seas helps weaken waves before they reach the shore.

“The study shows beautifully how atolls are an intimately interconnected island-reef system, a geo-ecological system,” said Yadvinder Malhi, an ecologist at the University of Oxford and a co-author.

Parrotfish scrape coral and excrete it as sand. On some Indian Ocean reefs they produce up to 85 percent of the new sand.

Around islands with seabirds, parrotfish had more energy available, and the surrounding reefs produced 2.3 to 2.8 times as much sand.

In an interview with Earth.com, Graham was asked what surprised him most.

“The increase in sediment production by seabirds was something that had not been investigated before, and the increase is quite dramatic,” he said.

He put a figure on it for a hypothetical island of about 35 acres (14 hectares), roughly three quarters of a mile long.

With seabirds present, the surrounding reefs would produce about 220 cubic yards (170 cubic meters) more sediment each year than reefs around an island without seabirds. That’s roughly 20 dump truck loads.

“That is a really meaningful quantity,” Graham said.

Not all of that sand reaches the beach. The grains on the reef and the grains on the shore match closely, though, which points to a steady supply.

On Tetiaroa, the team measured fine roots in forest plots for two years.

Where native trees such as Pisonia grandis covered more than 75 percent of the ground, each square yard of soil held an estimated 8.2 miles (13.2 kilometers) of fine root.

Where native cover was below 75 percent, the figure was 1.8 miles (2.9 kilometers).

Coconut palms have short, rounded root systems. Native broadleaf trees grow long, dense roots that hold sand in place when storm waves wash over an island.

Seabirds strengthened that effect. With plenty of bird nitrogen in the soil, root growth rose by about 9 percent for every extra 1% of native forest cover. With few birds, more native forest didn’t change root growth at all.

The reef growth and sand figures come from six islands in the Chagos Archipelago, and the root figures from 19 forest plots on five islands of Tetiaroa.

The team inferred the gains from islands that already differ, rather than following one atoll from rat eradication through to a faster-growing reef.

How much reef sand actually reaches an island, and how reef growth changes the scouring of a shoreline, still have to be measured. Island size and local currents also shape what happens to any one atoll.

Jennifer Appoo, a co-author at the University of Seychelles, said the results matter most where seawalls and other engineering are unaffordable or out of place.

Many of the Seychelles’ atolls are uninhabited or sparsely inhabited, she said.

Graham told Earth.com that eradicating invasive predators such as rats should be the top priority for island managers.

It helps the island’s wildlife and the reef around it, he said, and this study shows it can boost the islands’ climate resilience too.

“I think what is key here from a policy perspective is that restoring atoll islands can have major gains in two core areas: biodiversity conservation, and climate adaptation,” he said.

Rats have already been removed from about 1,000 islands worldwide.

Asked by Earth.com which islands he is watching next, Graham said he has just started an Island-Ocean Research Hub at Lancaster.

It will study islands from the tropics to the Arctic, in the Seychelles, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean, the U.K. and Arctic Norway.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6348. Wildlife experts rescued over 90 venomous primates that were supposed to be extinct for nearly a century

The critically endangered Bangka slow loris has been rediscovered in Indonesia after decades without scientific records, but its habitat remains at risk.

The Bangka slow loris, a small venomous primate that had not appeared in the scientific literature since the 1930s, still lives on Bangka Island in Indonesia. The species is listed as Critically Endangered, and possibly extinct, on the IUCN Red List.

Between 2015 and 2025, the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center on Bangka rescued more than 90 of the animals. It released 86 of them back into forests on the island.

Staff at the center published those records in October 2026, in a study with partners from zoos in Austria and Indonesia. The conservation group Re:wild announced the findings.

The Bangka slow loris, Nycticebus bancanus, was described in 1906 from Kelabat Bay on Bangka. For decades it was treated as a subspecies of other slow lorises, until a 2013 study raised it to a species of its own.

The IUCN Red List gives 1937 as the year the loris was last recorded, a date the authors trace to a 1937 publication describing three adult males. Museum material suggests those specimens may date from 1930 to 1932, so the last record could be older still.

Re:wild lists the Bangka slow loris among the most wanted primates in its search for lost species.

Benji Barca, the exploration program manager at Re:wild, credited the rescue center’s work.

“The team at Alobi has spent more than a decade quietly rescuing, healing and releasing these animals, and their careful records are what have finally now brought this primate back into scientific view,” Barca said.

“A species can disappear from the scientific record without disappearing from the lives of the people who share its home,” he noted.

The center kept detailed records for 43 lorises rescued from 2021 to August 2025. Sixteen were found in houses or gardens and six on roads, and at least three of the 43 died.

Seven had injuries suspected to come from electric shocks, and five came from captivity or the wildlife trade. Three turned up on plantations, one was caught in a fence and one was attacked by a dog.

Alobi rescued Bangka slow lorises in all four regencies of Bangka Island and in the city of Pangkal Pinang. That spread suggests the primate may still live across much of Bangka.

Timon Glaw of the Haus des Meeres Aqua Terra Zoo in Vienna, Austria, is the study’s corresponding author.

“We now know the species has survived in several parts of Bangka, and we urgently need a long-term conservation strategy built on population surveys, genetic studies and, above all, protection of its remaining habitat,” Glaw said.

“The next challenge is to make sure it does not actually become extinct,” he added.

The 86 released animals went to seven sites. Bukit Mangkol forest park received 37, Permisan nature park received 22 and the Mount Menumbing area received 15.

The four other sites took six, three, two and one animal. They include Gunung Maras National Park and the BIO protected forest.

How many of the released lorises survived over the long term is not yet known, because no follow-up data exist.

The authors call for future releases of rescued slow lorises to be monitored, as part of an in situ conservation program that protects suitable habitat.

Slow lorises are the only primates known to be venomous. They lick a gland on the inside of the upper arm and mix its secretion with saliva, producing a bite that can be painful and cause swelling.

The venom’s main role in nature seems to be defense against parasites and against other lorises, a 2013 review of slow loris venom concluded.

In extreme cases, a bite can send a person into anaphylactic shock, which has sometimes proved fatal.

In a preliminary test, leeches placed in contact with a mix of the gland oil and saliva all died.

Langka Sani, who leads the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center and co-authored the study, points to habitat loss as the main danger.

“We are glad to contribute to the scientific record to show that the Bangka slow loris is not lost, but the species is still very close to extinction,” Sani explained.

“Its natural habitat on Bangka Island has shrunk significantly because of illegal tin mining and massive land clearing for oil palm plantations.”

Forest habitat on Bangka fell by 62 percent between 2000 and 2012, according to a 2017 analysis by Supriatna and colleagues cited in the paper.

Settlements, roads, power lines and the pet trade also threaten the loris, Re:wild noted. Five of the rescued animals had been kept in captivity or caught up in the wildlife trade, even though slow lorises are protected by law.

The authors also recommend a conservation breeding program, molecular studies to confirm its identity and targeted surveys on Bangka, Belitung and Borneo. They ask the IUCN to reassess the loris, especially its “Possibly Extinct” tag.

The study was published in the journal Spixiana.

#6347. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

#6346. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 3: The Moon passes Regulus

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 2: The Moon passes Jupiter and Mars

The Moon now passes 0.8° south of the bright star Regulus in Leo at 4 A.M. EST. Some regions of the world will see our satellite pass in front of Regulus in an occultation, but again, the event is not visible from North America.

The pair rises together shortly after midnight on the 2nd, following Jupiter and Mars by roughly an hour. By 5 A.M. local time on the 3rd, the Moon-star pair is nearly 50° high in the southeast. Despite its brightness (it is ranked as the 21st brightest star in the sky), magnitude 1.4 Regulus will be the faintest object in this region, as magnitude 0.8 Mars and magnitude –2.0 Jupiter to its west (upper right) far outshine it.

The waning Moon has shrunk from roughly 43% lit yesterday morning to 33% lit today. It is just under a week from New phase, which occurs on the 9th. Between now and then, the phase will continue to diminish and the Moon will rise later in the morning each day, until it travels across the sky in tandem with the Sun when it is New.

Venus passes 2° south of Spica at 8 A.M. EST this morning — they’ll be in the same configuration tomorrow morning, so keep reading below for details on how to observe them.

Sunrise: 6:31 A.M.Sunset: 4:55 P.M.Moonrise: 12:34 A.M.Moonset: 2:07 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (26%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon high above them in Leo, creating a gorgeous sight that early risers won’t want to miss.

By 6 A.M. local time (roughly half an hour before sunrise), the sky is growing bright and Venus and Spica are about 8° high in the east. Venus, at magnitude –4.4, far outshines the magnitude 1.0 star, which sits just to the planet’s upper left. A waning crescent Moon, just over 20% lit, hangs high above the pair, to their upper right. Through a telescope, Venus’ large, 58”-wide disk is also a crescent, now 5% lit. In the coming days, Venus’ phase will start to grow as its diameter slowly shrinks.

Also glance to Venus and Spica’s upper left, where you’ll spot magnitude –0.1 Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes the Herdsman, which borders Virgo to the north.

#6345. A couple walking their dog spotted a rusty can and found 1,427 buried gold coins

A California couple discovered 1,427 gold coins buried in eight rusty cans on their property in 2013, uncovering a treasure worth over $10 million.

In 2013, a Northern California couple known only as John and Mary were walking their dog on their property when they noticed a rusty can poking out of the ground. It was the first of eight cans that together held 1,427 gold coins.

The coins were struck between 1847 and 1894 and had a face value of $27,980. Kagin’s, Inc., the coin firm that marketed the find, estimated the coin hoard‘s value at more than $10 million.

“We found the coins buried on a little area of our property that we call the Saddle Ridge,” Mary said in an interview with the couple. The treasure became known as the Saddle Ridge Hoard.

“I saw an old can sticking out of the ground on a trail that we had walked almost every day for many, many years,” John recalled.

“John used a stick to dig up the first can,” Mary explained.

Carrying the can toward the house, the couple stopped for a breather because it was so heavy. John joked that it must be full of lead paint.

“Right after making the comment about it possibly being paint, the lid cracked off and exposed a rib of a single gold coin,” he recounted.

“Of course, it was a very surreal moment,” John noted of his first reaction.

Back at the trail, about a foot (30 centimeters) to the left of the first can, the couple broke into a second one with a small hand shovel.

In all, the coins lay in eight decaying metal canisters, all less than a foot (30 centimeters) beneath the surface.

The cans were numbered and had been placed in a curious alignment with the North Star, the American Numismatic Association reported.

“Years ago, on our first hike, we noticed an old tree growing into the hill,” John recalled in the association’s account. An unusual angular rock also sat up the hill from where the coins were buried.

“Starting at the rock, if you walk 10 paces towards the North Star, you wind up smack in the middle of the coins!” Mary pointed out.

For safekeeping at first, John hid the coins at home. “I dug a hole under the wood pile and got a slab of green board to cover it,” he remembered.

Most of the gold coins were $20 Liberty double eagles struck at the San Francisco Mint from 1855 to 1894, according to the Professional Coin Grading Service (PCGS), which certified each coin.

Kagin’s counted almost 1,400 $20 gold pieces, 50 $10 gold pieces and four $5 gold pieces in the hoard.

The $20 coin dates to the California Gold Rush. An 1849 example was the first $20 coin struck by the U.S. Mint during that rush, according to the Smithsonian Institution.

David Hall, co-founder of PCGS, called the hoard “a literal time capsule” of coins that circulated in the late 19th century. In 2014, more than a dozen of its coins ranked as the finest known, or tied for finest known, in the PCGS Population Report.

One of them, an 1866-S “No Motto” double eagle, was valued at around $1 million.

David McCarthy, senior numismatist at Kagin’s, evaluated the coins after the couple contacted him. “Many pieces were finer than anything known in major collections or museums,” he observed.

Based on the coins’ dates and condition, along with the decay of the cans, Kagin’s concluded that the hoard was buried over a significant period of time in the late 19th century.

“Unlike other hoards and treasures, this one includes a great variety of dates, many of which are in pristine condition,” noted Donald Kagin, president of Kagin’s.

Who did the burying remains unknown. One idea links the coins to a robbery of the San Francisco Mint in 1901, but the wide range of coin conditions has put that theory to rest.

Other suggestions include a secret society or a landowner hiding gold around the time of Franklin D. Roosevelt’s gold confiscation order. Neither idea has been confirmed.

About 90 percent of the coins were to be sold through Amazon’s collectibles store, in what Kagin’s called the first major numismatic treasure sold there. Others were sold through Kagin’s own platform.

Before the sale, a sample of the coins went on display at the American Numismatic Association’s National Money Show in Atlanta, from February 27 to March 1, 2014.

With the proceeds, John and Mary paid off personal debt and donated to local charities.

“We love our lives as they are – I hope we can help our family members and our community and give back some,” Mary told the interviewer.

Before Saddle Ridge, the largest reported buried gold find in the U.S. had a face value of $4,500. Construction workers found it in Jackson, Tennessee, in 1985, and it later sold for around $1 million.

The information was obtained from the American Numismatic Association.

The sale of the Nanotyrannus "Jodi" for over $47 million shines a stark light on the commodification of Earth's history. By selling dinosaurs off to the highest bidder, we lose what makes them valuable in the first place.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dinosaurs are more than extraordinary specimens with massive price tags. They are irreplaceable snapshots of our planet's history and our own human journey. When scientifically important fossils are reduced to luxury commodities, we are robbed of the evidence that makes them valuable in the first place.

On Oct. 27, a 19.6-foot-long (6 meters) skeleton of Nanotyrannus lancensis known as "Jodi" was sold at Sotheby's in New York for $47,255,000, far exceeding its $6 million to $9 million estimate. The buyer and seller were not identified. It was the latest in a string of multimillion-dollar dinosaur auctions, following the $50.1 million sale of a T. rex (Gus) in July and the $44.6 million sale of a Stegosaurus (Apex) in 2024.

Fossils like Jodi, Apex, and Gus belong in public collections, where they can contribute to science and remain accessible for future generations. Not in the hands of private collectors.

There are three main reasons why. First: Fossils are evidence, not objects. A dinosaur's bones can reveal how it grew, moved, fed, and lived. They preserve traces of injury and disease, help reconstruct ancient ecosystems, and offer clues about the "rules of life" governing our world that scientists are still learning to interpret.

Jodi illustrates exactly why access to physical evidence matters. For nearly half a century, paleontologists debated whether Nanotyrannus was a distinct dinosaur or simply a juvenile T. rex. A lack of well-preserved fossils available for study only fueled the uncertainty. And then a remarkable specimen, once in private hands, moved into the public trust.

The fossil was uncovered in Montana in 2006 alongside a Triceratops. Dubbed the "Dueling Dinosaurs," it took until 2022, and an appeal in the state's Supreme Court, for the remains to be acquired by the Museum of Natural Sciences so they could be fully studied. This research provided a powerful new perspective, arguing that Nanotyrannus lancensis was a distinct dinosaur and, moreover, that a second species of Nanotyrannus once roamed the American West.

When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow.

This hypothesis has big implications for the health of ecosystems before one of Earth's most severe extinction events — but it currently rests on the scant few Nanotyrannus specimens housed in public collections. Specimens like Jodi could uphold or dethrone it. Without access, we, and Jodi’s true identity, will remain in the dark.

It is hard to overstate the irony of Jodi's sale: a specimen recently listed as a juvenile T. rex now captures the world's imagination, and commands double the price tag, as a "Nanotyrannus." Yet if a similar fate had befallen the Dueling Dinosaurs and they had remained in private hands, we would not have known for certain that Nanotyrannus ever existed.

Scientific progress depends on researchers being able to compare specimens, test hypotheses, and revisit earlier conclusions. When access relies on a private owner's permission, repeatability is not assured, and science cannot proceed. A specimen might be available today but inaccessible tomorrow. This is why access to the evidence must endure.

This brings us to the second problem with privately owned dinosaurs. Digital scans cannot replace the original fossil.

Three-dimensional scans and digital models are powerful tools. We use them to measure bones, compare anatomy, share information, and educate the public. But digital models capture only the most superficial aspects of a fossil's story.

The auction took place on Oct. 27, with Jodi eventually selling for around five times the top estimate.

To understand dinosaur growth, we examine microscopic structures inside fossilized bone through a technique called bone histology. We also analyze the chemistry of fossils to investigate diet, migration patterns, and metabolism. Such work requires physical samples, not just images of a bone's surface. We also need contextual data about the surrounding sediments, preservation mode, and ancient environment in order to explore questions about the ecosystems in which the animals once lived. Much of this information is lost in the rush to excavate and prepare fossils as quickly as possible for the auction block. It can never be reclaimed.

We cannot predict what novel technologies future researchers will employ to make new discoveries from old bones, or even which questions they will ask. Technology will continue to advance, bringing analytical methods we cannot anticipate. A scan made today does not guarantee that researchers will have the physical evidence needed for tomorrow's discoveries. Digital access should complement preservation of original specimens, not justify losing it.

Finally, private ownership cannot guarantee lasting public access. Yes, some private collectors financially support research and education and donate specimens they purchase. Those contributions are valuable. But the issue is not whether an individual owner is generous; it is whether access is guaranteed over time.

A temporary loan is insufficient. A loaned specimen can be withdrawn, sold, or inherited by someone with different priorities, situations that are becoming increasingly common in the U.S. and abroad. By contrast, a fossil deposited in a responsible public research institution is documented, cared for, studied, and made available to future researchers and educators in perpetuity. The question is not whether people should be able to admire dinosaurs; it is whether the evidence that helps us understand them will remain available to everyone.

Nor should museums consider selling scientifically important fossils to cover operating shortfalls. Collections are not ordinary financial assets to liquidate when budgets tighten. Selling an irreplaceable specimen provides a one-time payment while sacrificing future scientific potential. Museums need sustainable funding for collections care, research, and education, not pressure to trade away the very resources they exist to preserve.

Jodi's sale is complete, but the fossil's long-term future remains uncertain. With the buyer's identity undisclosed, the public cannot know what arrangements, if any, will ensure continued access for researchers and educators. We hope the new owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education, through permanent placement in a public research institution. But hope is not a substitute for a guarantee.

There is a better way to support paleontology. Enthusiasts who want to share in the excitement of discovery can fund fieldwork and research, endow curatorial positions, strengthen museum collections, or donate important fossils to public institutions where we can all learn from them.

Dinosaurs inspire wonder because they connect us to a world vastly different from our own. But their importance extends far beyond their power to captivate us. They are part of our shared natural heritage and an irreplaceable record of Earth's history.

We should measure a dinosaur's worth not by the price it commands at auction, but by the knowledge it can help us build, and by whether we preserve that opportunity for generations to come. Earth's history belongs to all of us, not to the highest bidder.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Nov. 4 at 8.22 a.m. ET to correct the year the Museum of Natural Sciences acquired the Dueling Dinosaurs.

#6342. Crocodylians rather than mammals were the top hunters in their ancient habitat

Fossil bite marks reveal that giant crocodylians were likely the leading predators of huge mammals about 12 million years ago

South America looked very different during the Middle Miocene, roughly 11 to 13 million years ago. In what is now Colombia, rivers and wetlands were home to giant turtles, fish, snakes, huge plant-eating mammals, flightless terror birds, carnivorous mammals, and many kinds of crocodylians.

Crocodylians include living crocodiles, alligators, and caimans, along with their extinct relatives.

New fossil evidence suggests that these reptiles were likely the leading predators of the largest land mammals in this tropical community.

The fossils came from La Venta in Colombia’s Tatacoa Desert.

Mammalian predators lived there too, but there were not many of them, so other large predators, like crocodylians, played an important role.

Oscar Wilson, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki, worked with colleagues to examine this puzzle using direct physical evidence.

Earlier work had predicted a major role for giant crocodylians by comparing the combined body masses of predators and prey.

“There was so much prey available that mammalian predators couldn’t have eaten it all,” Wilson said.

“Our new study shows that crocodylians in particular were the region’s most important predators, especially when it came to hunting large prey.”

The team studied four fossils from three types of large plant-eating mammals that once lived in South America. These animals were similar in some ways to the large hoofed mammals that live today.

The main evidence came from marks that other animals left on the bones. These included deep tooth marks, small dents, grooves, cracks, and crushed areas.

The researchers photographed each fossil and created 3D digital models of several specimens. They also used a CT scan on one jaw to see inside the fossil without cutting or damaging it.

They measured the bite marks and compared them with fossil teeth.

The researchers also estimated how much force was needed to make the marks in fresh bone. This information helped them identify the most likely predators.

One Pericotoxodon skull carried a nearly circular puncture about 1.15 inches (29.2 millimeters) wide, along with smaller pits and grooves.

A leg bone from the same species held five deep punctures and four shallow pits, showing that several teeth had contacted the bone.

A Xenastrapotherium lower jaw had two large punctures surrounded by fractures and heavily crushed areas. The marks passed through the hard outer layer of bone, pointing to a powerful bite delivered while the bone was fresh.

A young Granastrapotherium jaw also showed punctures, crushed bone, and drag marks from teeth.

One sharply curved groove may record violent movement, such as shaking, thrashing, or the rolling motion used by living crocodiles during feeding.

The animals’ estimated weights ranged from about 1,360 to 4,020 pounds (616 to 1,822 kilograms). However, some body mass estimates came from tooth measurements, a method that may overestimate the size of these unusual extinct mammals.

The strongest match was Purussaurus neivensis, a giant relative of modern caimans that may have reached about 23 feet in length and weighed close to 3,950 pounds.

Its front teeth were thick and conical, with some measured adult teeth reaching about 1.7 inches (43.7 millimeters) wide at the base.

Their size and rounded shape closely matched the largest punctures, while ridges along some tooth edges could account for marks that split into two points.

Other local crocodylians had teeth that were too small, too oval, or too flat and serrated to fit the main wounds.

Combined estimates from several punctures exceeded 9,000 pounds of force (40,000 newtons) and sometimes approached 15,700 pounds of force (70,000 newtons).

The estimate from the skull was probably too high because the tooth passed through thinner bone than that found in the jaws and leg bone.

“The frequency of marks likely made by Purussaurus suggests that it was an important predator in these tropical ecosystems,” Wilson said.

Fossils rarely reveal whether a predator killed an animal or scavenged it after death, and these bones cannot answer that question with certainty.

None showed signs of healing, which rules out wounds that had begun to repair. However, that fact alone does not distinguish hunting from scavenging.

Three damaged fossils came from the head, while the fourth came from the lower leg near the knee.

Living crocodiles often seize prey by the skull or legs during an ambush, and experiments with pig carcasses have produced skull damage similar to the marks on the Pericotoxodon fossil.

The curved mark on the Granastrapotherium jaw suggests that a predator fed on it using strong, violent movements. Missing pieces from two fossils may also have been torn away during feeding.

However, weathering, pressure during burial, or damage before collection could have destroyed those pieces. The Xenastrapotherium jaw may show signs of another feeding event.

Ten small, parallel grooves on the other side were probably made later by a smaller animal with serrated teeth. The researchers think Langstonia may have scavenged the remains.

Purussaurus may have waited near freshwater and attacked large mammals as they came to drink, much as large crocodiles hunt today.

Still, no living crocodylian reaches the same size, so modern species offer useful comparisons rather than perfect models.

As large predators, these reptiles may have carried nutrients from land into the water and left parts of their prey for turtles, fish, birds, and other animals to eat.

They may also have affected large herbivore populations, although the fossils do not prove that they controlled those populations.

The evidence comes from only four specimens, and the team found the marks by chance rather than through a systematic search of all La Venta collections.

A systematic survey could show whether crocodylian bites were common and whether different predators left recognizable patterns.

For now, these damaged bones offer the first direct evidence that giant crocodylians fed on some of the largest mammals at La Venta.

Purussaurus was likely an important predator, although some of the marks may have resulted from scavenging.

The study is published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

#6341. Nov. 3, 1957: The flight of Laika

Less than a month after the launch of Sputnik 1, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2. The mission was readied quickly in order to keep the propaganda momentum from Sputnik 1 and to coincide with the 40th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution.

Carrying mixed-breed dog Laika, Sputnik 2 was the first flight to carry a living animal to Earth orbit. A small stray from the Moscow streets, Laika had undergone training to help her become accustomed her to the close quarters and gravity changes. Electrodes attached to the dog sent data back to Earth, for future research into the biological effects of space travel. Unfortunately, Laika died a few hours after takeoff – always the expected outcome of the mission, as the life-support systems on Sputnik 2 were imperfect and there was no plan for recovering the satellite or its passenger after launch. Sputnik 2 burned up on reentry in 1958, after its batteries died the previous year. In 2008, a statue commemorating Laika was erected in Moscow.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6340. Older adults get tailored plans for fall prevention, but a simple leaflet may work just as well

Across 110 trials, tailored fall prevention plans for older people worked no better than basic advice, and people on them fell slightly more often.

A doctor who worries that an older patient might fall can order the full workup. Balance, eyesight and medicines get checked, someone looks at the loose rugs at home, and a plan is then built around those findings. It sounds like the gold standard of fall prevention.

However, pooled across the trials that have tested it, that tailored plan probably prevents no more falls than a leaflet of good advice. People on the plans actually fell slightly more often.

The result comes from a new Cochrane review, a kind of study that gathers every reliable trial on a question and pools the numbers. This one covered 110 trials and 48,919 people aged 60 and over. All participants were living at home rather than in care.

Lianne Wood and Cynthia Swarnalatha of the University of Exeter led the review. The co-authors were at the University of Oxford and the University of Sydney.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wood said the next job is to work out what the tailored programs contain that plain advice doesn’t.

“At the moment we are not sure why the results show that education is possibly more effective than tailored interventions,” she said.

Researchers call the tailored approach a multifactorial program. A health professional checks a person for two or more risks that can be changed, then treats or refers each one.

That might mean an exercise class for weak legs, a medicine review, or a handrail for the bathroom.

Seven trials with 9,901 people compared that approach with falls advice or education alone. The advice side was deliberately basic, often a standard leaflet such as Age U.K.’s Staying Steady, sent by post or handed over in a session.

People on the tailored plans had about 9 percent more falls per year than people given advice. The review rated that evidence as moderately certain. The chance of falling at least once, and of falling two or more times, was the same in both groups.

Against usual care, meaning no special fall prevention at all, the tailored plans did better, but not by much. Across 29 trials and 9,442 people, they cut the number of falls by about a quarter. In 17 trials, the risk of falling two or more times was about 13 percent lower.

The chance of falling at least once barely moved, across 38 trials and 12,774 people. Fall-related fractures and hospital stays didn’t change either.

The review rated all of those results as low-certainty evidence. This was because results varied from trial to trial and many trials had weaknesses in design.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most once the trials were pooled, Wood said it was what did not happen.

“We were surprised that there were no other big changes to the previous review, despite adding many more people and trials of higher quality,” she said. “Much of the pooled results are very similar to the 2018 review with low quality evidence.”

The review also tested the untailored version, called a multiple component program, in which everyone gets the same bundle, regardless of their own risks. Forty-four trials used that design, and one tested both approaches.

Against usual care, those bundles made little or no difference to the number of falls, though they may have lowered the chance of falling at least once by about 12 percent. Against exercise alone, and against advice alone, they made little or no difference on any measure.

Side effects were generally mild, mostly short-lived aches from exercise, and serious ones were rare.

The components themselves were familiar. Of the 66 tailored-program trials, 53 included home safety changes or assistive equipment, 49 included exercise, and 36 included a medicine review.

Wood was asked what a health service that runs these programs should do on Monday morning.

“So, until we know more, we’d advise people to continue as normal,” she told Earth.com.

Asked what the best evidence does support, she named two things. “We know that falls prevention education and advice to start with exercise appears to be effective, so this may be the area we need to put more emphasis on.”

Her view fits the direction guidelines have already taken. The 2025 guidance in the United Kingdom puts strength and balance training at the center of prevention, and the 2022 World Falls Guidelines call exercise a core intervention.

Exercise and standard advice may also take less time and money to roll out across a whole population than individual assessments.

The review pooled every tailored program together, so it can’t say whether some combinations of components work better than others. The authors wrote that this question needs a different kind of analysis.

In most trials, participants knew which group they were in, and most relied on people reporting their own falls. Six of the comparisons showed signs that trials with weak results were less likely to have been published.

Trials that counted harder outcomes, such as fractures, have generally shown disappointing results, the authors wrote.

The evidence also comes from a narrow slice of the world. The tailored-program trials came from 22 countries, but most were run in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Only 17 of those 66 trials reported participants’ ethnicity, and some trials excluded people with dementia.

“There still remains a real lack of studies in low to middle income countries and people of different ethnicities, so understanding the effects of treatments in these groups remains a real priority,” Wood said.

About one in three people over 65 fall at least once a year. In the United States alone, falls in that age group led to about 4.5 million emergency department visits in 2024, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Previous falls, muscle weakness and poor balance all raise the risk. A fall can also leave a fear of falling again, which the review links to faster physical decline and a retreat from social life.

Co-author Sarah Lamb of the University of Exeter said the results show how much is still unknown about why falls happen in the first place.

“We’re now conducting a major study to understand why people have unstable walking and are at higher risk of falls,” Lamb said.

“Combined with this review, it will help us design the best prevention programs in future, to reduce frailty and help people live well for as long as possible.”

Next, the authors want a single, large trial that tests home changes and exercise, alone and together, against usual care.

They also want wearable sensors recording falls instead of diaries. Until that trial runs, the pooled record says a tailored plan and a leaflet do about the same job, and nobody can yet say why.

The full study was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

#6339. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6336. A new species of millipede that loves moisture has been discovered living in a surprisingly dry part of South Australia

A post-fire survey on Kangaroo Island turned up a millipede first collected in 1936 and left unnamed for 90 years.

In Australia, entomologists had only ever found millipedes from the moisture-loving family Dalodesmidae in the wetter east and southwest. So a male collected in 1936 on a dry stretch of South Australia’s coast didn’t fit.

Ninety years later, that millipede finally has a name, Colobothrix deckeri. It’s the first of its family known from such a dry part of the country.

Robert Mesibov, a millipede specialist in Ulverstone, Tasmania, described the new genus and species after finding fresh specimens on nearby Kangaroo Island.

Until now, scientists had not described any dalodesmid anywhere in a stretch of more than 1,240 miles (2,000 kilometers) between western Victoria and southwest Western Australia.

Most of the southern half of the country inside that gap gets less than 16 inches (400 millimeters) of rain a year.

The entomologist Herbert Womersley collected the millipede on the lower Yorke Peninsula in April 1936, during a little-known scientific expedition based at Marion Bay.

The specimen went into the South Australian Museum as an unidentified millipede.

The millipede stayed unidentified until 2015. That year, the German millipede researcher Peter Decker borrowed many of the museum’s specimens for his Ph.D. work on a different millipede family.

He was then at the Senckenberg Museum of Natural History in Görlitz. Among the loaned specimens were fragments of Womersley’s male.

Decker recognized the male as a dalodesmid and sent microscope images to Mesibov, who specializes in that family. The new species carries Decker’s name for that reason.

A 2012 study used the term shelf life for the wait between collecting a new species and describing it. For Colobothrix deckeri, Mesibov wrote, that wait was 90 years.

In the southern winters of 2016 and 2017, Mesibov searched forest, woodland and scrub within about 12 miles (20 kilometers) of Marion Bay. He didn’t find the millipede, though the trips did produce a different new species.

By then, entomologists had already collected the animal somewhere else. In 2010, arachnologists Michael Rix and Danilo Harms were collecting spiders and other small animals on Kangaroo Island, about 31 miles (50 kilometers) south of Marion Bay.

At one site in the island’s relatively wet northwest corner, they found a new species of assassin spider.

Rix and Harms also collected two male and seven female millipedes there. The animals went to the Western Australian Museum. There Catherine Car, a specialist in millipedes and centipedes, identified them as dalodesmids.

They weren’t matched to the 1936 specimen for years.

Bushfires swept Kangaroo Island in 2020 and burned out the 2010 site. The assassin spider, Zephyrarchea austini, had been described from that single spot, and there were fears the fires had left it close to extinction.

In 2021, arachnologist Jessica Marsh ran a targeted survey for the spider. She found two more on private land about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) west of the original site, and the small animals she collected along the way included the millipede.

This year, while searching online for dalodesmid records in southern Australia, Mesibov found the Rix and Harms specimens in the Western Australian Museum’s online records.

Curator Mark Harvey sent close-up photos of one male, and its body and reproductive structures matched Womersley’s specimen.

Mesibov then traveled to Kangaroo Island. He couldn’t find the millipede at the 2010 site. He did identify it among the animals Marsh had collected.

“Third time lucky!” said Mesibov. “I found the new millipede alive and well this year at relatively wet sites not far from its 2010 and 2021 localities.”

An adult male Colobothrix deckeri is about 0.75 inches (19 millimeters) long, close to the width of a U.S. penny. Its yellowish-brown body is speckled with reddish brown. The feature that sets it apart is on the legs.

Mature males in this family, and in some other millipedes, carry tiny, ball-shaped structures called sphaerotrichomes. Normally, a long, pointed hair sticks out of each ball. In the new species, that hair is only a short, blunt rod, roughly a quarter the length of the ball.

So Mesibov named the genus Colobothrix, from Greek words meaning stunted hair. What the balls do in this group of millipedes is still unknown, he wrote.

Neither living nor preserved specimens gave off a strong smell. In Mesibov’s view, that suggests any defensive chemical the species makes releases only a little cyanide.

On Kangaroo Island, the millipede is known from five sites inside an area of about 23 square miles (60 square kilometers).

They’re in Flinders Chase National Park, in the Western River Wilderness Area and on private land along Snug Cove Road, and all of them have native woodland.

At the Flinders Chase site, modeled rainfall is about 32 inches (810 millimeters) a year.

Mesibov suggested that the species may once have lived across more of the island’s wetter western half. Farm clearing and frequent bushfires have removed or damaged much of the native woodland over the past two centuries, he wrote.

In the remaining patches near farms, introduced European millipedes now make up nearly all of the millipedes he has seen.

Mesibov’s paper also describes a second new species from the 2010 site, Notonesocambala adoceta. It’s a dark gray millipede up to about 2 inches (50 millimeters) long.

The biggest open question is whether Colobothrix deckeri still lives on the Yorke Peninsula.

Near Marion Bay, modeled rainfall is about 18 inches (450 millimeters) a year, well below the 24 to 31 inches (600 to 800 millimeters) modeled for northwestern Kangaroo Island.

“The 1936 locality is underlain by limestone,” said Mesibov, “and the rock is broken where it is exposed at the ground surface.”

He offered one possibility. “I wonder if the species survives in small voids in this bedrock, as a relict from wetter periods in South Australia’s past,” he said.

“That might explain why I couldn’t find it in 2016 and 2017, and how it could persist in such a dry climate.”

Researchers would have to find the millipede inside the rock to test that idea. Mesibov kept some of the new specimens for future genetic work.

He also wrote that other dalodesmids may still live on the nearby Fleurieu Peninsula.

He pointed to forest remnants in its wetter middle and to deep gullies in Deep Creek Conservation Park.

The full study was published in the journal ZooKeys.

The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

#6334. Cotton plants in poor soil lean on two hormones to grab enough potassium

Two plant hormones, ethylene and jasmonate, work together to help cotton take in potassium, and sprays of both raised yields in potassium-poor field soil.

Ethylene is the gas that ripens bananas on a kitchen counter, but in cotton plants it has a second job. Together with a partner hormone called jasmonate, it turns on the machinery that pulls potassium into the plant when the soil runs short.

Spraying cotton leaves with versions of both hormones also raised yields in potassium-poor field soil.

A team led by Professors Zhaohu Li and Xiaoli Tian at China Agricultural University in Beijing worked out the steps in upland cotton, Gossypium hirsutum.

Scientists recently traced the species’ origin to Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. The team describes the work as a possible basis for helping crops use potassium more efficiently.

The team tested its idea in two ways: lab experiments on the plant’s genes and proteins, and field experiments on cotton grown in potassium-deficient soil.

It ran the field work only in that kind of soil, so the field results don’t say whether the sprays would help where potassium is already plentiful.

Potassium helps plants run photosynthesis, switch on enzymes, and balance water inside their cells. Cotton is one crop that needs a lot of it. Researchers have found that more potassium is leaving agricultural soils around the world than is going back in.

Yet scientists understand less about how plants take up potassium than about nitrogen and phosphorus. In crops, the way genes control the proteins that carry potassium into cells remains largely unexplored. Other researchers have searched cotton’s genes for ways to make the crop tolerate drought.

The team started with the protein that does the work. It’s a transporter that carries potassium into the plant’s cells. This one grabs potassium even when little is around, and the plant needs it to keep its potassium level steady during a shortage.

A control protein switches the transporter’s gene on by attaching to the DNA right beside it. Two other proteins, one from the jasmonate pathway and one from the ethylene pathway, each attach to the DNA beside the control protein’s gene and turn it up. Then the two link up, and as a pair they turn up the control protein more than either one does alone.

In cotton, then, the two hormones act as partners rather than as separate signals. Hormones do plenty of jobs besides telling plants when to grow. In one earlier study, a drought hormone helped plants block spider mites.

A plant with enough potassium doesn’t need the extra uptake, and the team found how the plant keeps the system off.

When potassium is plentiful, two proteins that hold others back grab the jasmonate-pathway protein and the control protein. In the team’s reading, that stops the plant from spending resources on a system it doesn’t need.

Crops run a similar shutoff for nitrogen. Researchers recently found a protein that tells crops to stop absorbing nitrogen even when plenty remains in the soil.

To see whether the finding could matter on a farm, the team ran field experiments in soil with a shortage of potassium. Each kilogram of that soil held less than 60 milligrams of available potassium (60 parts per million). The team calls that a moderate-to-severe shortage.

The team sprayed cotton leaves with methyl jasmonate, a form of jasmonate, or with ACC, a compound plants turn into ethylene. Either spray raised the potassium level in the leaves and improved photosynthesis.

Using both did best. It raised seed cotton yield by 11.6% compared to unsprayed plants. Seed cotton is the crop as it comes off the plant, with the seeds still inside.

In the field, as in the lab, the two hormones worked best together.

The 11.6% gain came from soil with too little potassium, so it doesn’t show whether the sprays would help where potassium is already plentiful.

Anyone considering sprays like these on a working farm would first need to see the gain repeat across more fields and growing seasons.

The full study was published in the journal Science Bulletin.

#6333. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.
